justice: Spatial resources are heavily car-oriented: the entire corridor is essentially a single unmarked dirt roadway with no dedicated pedestrian sidewalk or cycling space.
Accessibility is weak because the surface is uneven dirt/gravel with ruts and loose material, creating barriers for strollers, wheelchairs, and anyone needing stable footing.
Fairness of use is limited by the lack of clear rules or delineation (no lane markings, no pedestrian priority zones), forcing all users to negotiate space with trucks on a narrow alignment.
safety: Narrow, winding rural road geometry with limited sight distance ahead increases conflict risk between the visible truck and any oncoming vehicles or slower users.
No edge protection: the road drops directly into vegetation on the right and left with no guardrail; only a single concrete block appears at the roadside, offering minimal safety containment.
Absence of crosswalks, shoulders, or separated paths means pedestrians/cyclists would be exposed to vehicle movements on the same dirt track.
livability: Lack of nearby buildings, shops, or active frontages suggests limited access to daily services and social activity along this segment.
No visible amenities (benches, lighting fixtures, shelters, trash bins) reduces the street’s suitability for lingering, rest, or social interaction for any road user.
The corridor functions more as a utility/rural access road (truck presence, dirt surface) than a place-oriented public space.
sustainability: High surrounding vegetation cover (dense trees and hillside greenery) contributes positively to local ecological value and potential air-quality benefits.
Unpaved dirt road likely reduces heat-island effect compared with large asphalt surfaces, though it may create dust impacts depending on traffic.
Overhead power lines and a utility pole indicate basic infrastructure provision without additional land-intensive installations in the corridor.
aesthetics: Expansive natural landscape views (forested hills and open sky) create strong scenic quality.
Dense roadside greenery and tree canopy on the left provides a visually rich, natural edge condition.
Visual clutter is relatively low aside from overhead wires and the utility pole, maintaining a predominantly natural character.
comfort: Thermal comfort is mixed: trees on the left provide some shade, but the roadway itself is largely exposed under open sky, which can be hot and glaring in daytime.
Physical comfort is limited by the uneven dirt surface and lack of dedicated walking/cycling pavement, increasing fatigue and discomfort for non-motorized users.
Psychological comfort may be reduced by isolation (few people/activities visible) and the presence of large vehicles (truck) on a narrow shared track.
walkability: No sidewalk or shoulder is visible; pedestrians would need to walk in the vehicle track, reducing perceived and actual walkability.
Unpaved, uneven dirt surface and encroaching vegetation at the edges make walking less stable and less continuous.
No pedestrian wayfinding, crossings, or lighting elements are present, limiting route legibility and all-day usability.
bikeability: No bike lane markings, protection, or shoulder space; cyclists must share a narrow dirt road with trucks and other vehicles.
Loose/uneven unpaved surface increases slipping risk and reduces cycling comfort and control, especially on curves.
Roadway width and edge conditions (vegetation drop-off, minimal barriers) provide little recovery space for cyclists avoiding vehicles.
